answer_text:
For \(i<j\),

\[
P_i(x)+P_j(x)=2x^2+(b_i+b_j)x+(c_i+c_j).
\]

This quadratic has exactly one real root iff its discriminant is zero:

\[
(b_i+b_j)^2-8(c_i+c_j)=0,
\]

so for every pair \(i\ne j\),

\[
(b_i+b_j)^2=8(c_i+c_j). \tag{1}
\]

Now suppose \(n\ge 4\), and choose four distinct indices \(i,j,k,\ell\).

Apply (1) to \((i,k)\) and \((j,k)\):

\[
(b_i+b_k)^2=8(c_i+c_k),\qquad (b_j+b_k)^2=8(c_j+c_k).
\]

Subtracting gives

\[
(b_i-b_j)(b_i+b_j+2b_k)=8(c_i-c_j). \tag{2}
\]

Similarly, applying (1) to \((i,\ell)\) and \((j,\ell)\) gives

\[
(b_i-b_j)(b_i+b_j+2b_\ell)=8(c_i-c_j). \tag{3}
\]

Subtracting (2) and (3),

\[
2(b_i-b_j)(b_k-b_\ell)=0.
\]

Thus either \(b_i=b_j\) or \(b_k=b_\ell\).

- If \(b_i=b_j\), then from (1) applied to \((i,k)\) and \((j,k)\), we get \(c_i=c_j\), so \(P_i=P_j\), contradiction.
- If \(b_k=b_\ell\), then from (1) applied to \((i,k)\) and \((i,\ell)\), we get \(c_k=c_\ell\), so \(P_k=P_\ell\), contradiction.

Therefore \(n\le 3\).

It remains to show \(n=3\) is possible. Take

\[
P_1=x^2-4,\qquad P_2=x^2+4x+6,\qquad P_3=x^2+8x+12.
\]

Then

\[
P_1+P_2=2(x+1)^2,
\]
\[
P_1+P_3=2(x+2)^2,
\]
\[
P_2+P_3=2(x+3)^2,
\]

each having exactly one real root. Hence the maximum value is

\[
\boxed{3}
\]
